articleHeader.title: What is SQL (Structured Query Language)?
articleHeader.subtitle: A complete beginner-friendly guide to SQL — covering history, features, how SQL query execution works, database engines, DDL/DML/DCL/TCL, joins, normalization, Hello World query, and why SQL remains the universal language of data in 2026.

blocks.text: SQL (Structured Query Language) is a domain-specific language used to create, read, update, and manage data stored in relational database management systems (RDBMS). It was originally developed in the early 1970s at IBM by researchers Donald D. Chamberlin and Raymond F. Boyce, who called their early version SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language), built to manipulate data described by Edgar F. Codd's revolutionary relational model.

Unlike a general-purpose language such as Python or Rust, SQL is declarative — you describe what data you want, not how to fetch it step by step. You write SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country = 'India', and the database engine's internal query optimizer figures out the fastest execution plan to retrieve exactly that data.

SQL is both a standardized language and an ecosystem of database engines that implement it. The core syntax is standardized by ANSI and ISO/IEC 9075, but every major database — MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle Database, and SQLite — adds its own extensions and optimizations on top of that shared foundation, which is why SQL skills transfer easily between systems even though no two engines are perfectly identical.

According to the Stack Overflow Developer Survey and DB-Engines rankings, SQL-based databases continue to dominate the industry, and SQL itself is consistently ranked among the most widely used languages by professional developers — not as a competitor to languages like Python or JavaScript, but as an essential companion skill used alongside them in nearly every backend, data engineering, analytics, and business intelligence role.

The story of SQL begins with Edgar F. "Ted" Codd, a researcher at IBM, who in 1970 published a landmark paper titled "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks". Codd proposed organizing data into tables of rows and columns governed by mathematical set theory — a radical departure from the hierarchical and network databases common at the time. IBM assembled a research team to build a practical query language around Codd's model.

items.text: — Edgar F. Codd publishes his relational model paper at IBM, laying the theoretical foundation for what would become SQL.
— Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce at IBM develop SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language) as part of IBM's System R research project.
— Relational Software, Inc. (later renamed Oracle) releases Oracle V2, the first commercially available SQL-based relational database, beating IBM's own product to market.
— SQL is formally standardized for the first time by ANSI as SQL-86, giving the industry a shared baseline syntax across vendors.
— ISO adopts the ANSI standard internationally, cementing SQL as a globally recognized language rather than a single vendor's product.
— SQL-89 and the much larger SQL-92 (SQL2) standards are released, adding integrity constraints, joins, and significantly expanded functionality.
— SQL:1999 introduces recursive queries, triggers, and rudimentary object-oriented features, reflecting SQL's growing maturity.
— Successive standards (SQL:2003, SQL:2008, SQL:2011, SQL:2016) add window functions, XML support, temporal tables, and JSON functions.
— SQL:2023 is ratified, formally standardizing native JSON data type support and property graph query features across compliant engines.

— Modern cloud-native databases (Snowflake, Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, PostgreSQL 17+) continue extending SQL with vector search, semi-structured data support, and distributed query engines built for massive analytical workloads.

blocks.text: SQL's five-decade dominance is no accident. Its design balances mathematical rigor with an approachable, English-like syntax. Here are the 13 core features that define SQL:

items.title: Declarative & Readable
items.text: SQL statements read almost like English sentences — SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 18 tells the database exactly what you want without specifying how to retrieve it.

items.title: Relational Data Model
items.text: Data is organized into tables (relations) of rows and columns, linked through keys — a structure grounded in mathematical set theory that guarantees consistency and eliminates redundancy.

items.title: ACID Transactions
items.text: SQL databases support Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability — guaranteeing that transactions either fully complete or fully roll back, even during crashes or concurrent access.

items.title: Standardized Language
items.text: SQL is standardized by ANSI/ISO (SQL:2023 being the latest), so core syntax like SELECT, JOIN, and WHERE works consistently across MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and Oracle.

items.title: Powerful Joins
items.text: SQL can combine rows from multiple tables using INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL joins, letting you model and query complex relationships between entities like customers and orders.

items.title: Aggregate Functions
items.text: Built-in functions like COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX combined with GROUP BY let you summarize massive datasets into meaningful business insights in a single query.

items.title: Data Integrity Constraints
items.text: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, and CHECK constraints are enforced by the database itself, preventing invalid or inconsistent data from ever being stored.

items.title: Query Optimizer
items.text: Every SQL engine includes a cost-based query optimizer that automatically chooses the fastest execution plan — using indexes, join order, and statistics — without the developer writing low-level access code.

items.title: DDL, DML, DCL & TCL
items.text: SQL is organized into sub-languages: DDL defines structure (CREATE, ALTER), DML manipulates data (SELECT, INSERT), DCL controls access (GRANT, REVOKE), and TCL manages transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK).

items.title: Window Functions
items.text: Modern SQL supports window functions like ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and running totals via OVER(), enabling advanced analytics without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does.

items.title: Recursive Queries
items.text: Common Table Expressions (CTEs) with the RECURSIVE keyword let SQL traverse hierarchical data such as org charts, category trees, and bill-of-materials structures.

items.title: Massive Ecosystem
items.text: From SQLite on mobile apps to PostgreSQL for startups to distributed engines like Snowflake and BigQuery for petabyte-scale analytics — SQL scales from a single file to global data warehouses.

items.title: Multi-Paradigm Data Types
items.text: Modern SQL engines natively support JSON, arrays, geospatial data, and full-text search alongside traditional numeric, text, and date types — bridging relational and semi-structured data.

blocks.text: Key insight: The query optimizer is the real brain of a SQL database. Two logically identical queries — one using a subquery, another using a JOIN — can produce completely different performance because the optimizer picks execution strategies based on indexes, table statistics, and estimated row counts, not the literal order you typed your clauses in.

sections.title: How SQL Works — Database Engines, the SQL Standard, and Client Tools

blocks.text: Understanding the database engine, the SQL standard, and client tools is one of the first — and most important — concepts for every SQL beginner. These three pieces form the foundation of every SQL-based workflow, similar in spirit to how a language's compiler, its formal specification, and its developer tooling work together.
🗄️ Database Engine (RDBMS) — Where SQL Actually Runs

A database engine (also called an RDBMS — Relational Database Management System) is the actual software that stores your data and executes SQL against it. Popular engines include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle Database, and SQLite. When you run a query, it is the engine's parser, optimizer, and storage layer doing the actual work — SQL itself is just the language you use to talk to it.
📐 The SQL Standard — ANSI/ISO SQL

The SQL standard, maintained jointly by ANSI and ISO/IEC (as ISO/IEC 9075), defines the core syntax and behaviour that every compliant database engine should support — things like SELECT, JOIN, and GROUP BY. The current version is SQL:2023. No engine implements the standard 100% identically, and each adds its own vendor-specific extensions, which is why moving between MySQL and PostgreSQL feels similar but not always seamless.

items.html: SELECT * FROM customers; — retrieves every column and row from the customers table
CREATE TABLE orders (...) — defines a brand-new table structure
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (...) — adds a new row of data into a table
UPDATE orders SET status='shipped' WHERE id=1; — modifies existing rows matching a condition
DELETE FROM orders WHERE id=1; — removes rows matching a condition

blocks.text: 🖥️ Client Tools — Talking to the Database

Client tools are how developers and analysts actually send SQL to the engine and view results. Examples include the command-line psql for PostgreSQL, MySQL Workbench, SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), and cross-database GUI tools like DBeaver and TablePlus. Application code typically connects using a driver or ORM (like SQLAlchemy in Python or Prisma in Node.js) rather than a manual GUI tool.

Simple rule to remember: the database engine executes your SQL. The SQL standard defines the shared language you write it in. Client tools are how you send that SQL and see the results. The most widely adopted engines in 2026 remain PostgreSQL and MySQL for general-purpose workloads, with Snowflake and BigQuery leading large-scale cloud analytics.

sections.title: SQL vs Other Data Languages — Comparison

blocks.text: How does SQL compare to other languages and technologies used for working with data? This table gives you a quick side-by-side comparison to help you understand where SQL excels and where other tools take over.

Like every technology, SQL has remarkable strengths and real limitations. Understanding both helps you decide when a relational database is the right fit and when another data model might serve you better.

pros.title: Universally Standardized
pros.text: Core SQL syntax works across MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server, so the skills you learn transfer almost anywhere data is stored relationally.

pros.title: Guarantees Data Integrity
pros.text: Constraints, foreign keys, and ACID transactions ensure your data stays accurate and consistent, even under heavy concurrent access.

pros.title: Extremely Powerful for Complex Queries
pros.text: Joins, subqueries, window functions, and CTEs let you answer sophisticated business questions in a single, readable statement.

pros.title: Mature & Battle-Tested
pros.text: With over 50 years of real-world use, SQL databases power everything from small apps to the world's largest banks and airlines.

pros.title: Excellent Tooling & Ecosystem
pros.text: GUI clients, ORMs, BI tools like Tableau and Power BI, and cloud-managed database services make working with SQL approachable at every skill level.

pros.title: Huge Job Market
pros.text: SQL is one of the most requested skills across data analyst, data engineer, backend developer, and business intelligence roles worldwide.

pros.title: Scales From Tiny to Massive
pros.text: The same language works for a single-file SQLite mobile app and a petabyte-scale Snowflake data warehouse.

pros.title: Free & Open Source Options Available
pros.text: PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite are free, open-source, production-grade databases with zero licensing cost.

cons.title: Rigid Schema Requirements
cons.text: Relational databases require you to define a schema upfront; handling rapidly changing or deeply nested data can feel cumbersome compared to NoSQL.

cons.title: Vertical Scaling Limitations
cons.text: Traditional relational databases scale best by adding more power to a single server; horizontal scaling across many machines is harder than with NoSQL systems.

cons.title: Vendor Dialect Differences
cons.text: Despite the ANSI standard, functions and syntax quirks differ between MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server, so 100% portability is rarely guaranteed.

cons.title: Not Ideal for Unstructured Data
cons.text: Storing highly variable or document-like data (chat logs, sensor blobs) is often more natural in a NoSQL database or a JSON-native store.

cons.title: Complex Queries Can Be Hard to Read
cons.text: Deeply nested subqueries and multi-table joins can become difficult to write, debug, and optimize without solid SQL experience.

cons.title: Not a General-Purpose Language
cons.text: SQL cannot handle application logic, loops, or complex control flow on its own — it is almost always paired with another language like Python or Java.

sections.title: Where is SQL Used? — Real-World Applications

blocks.text: SQL's precision and reliability make it the backbone of virtually every data-driven system in the world. Here are the major areas where SQL is actively used in 2026:

items.text: — Core banking platforms rely on SQL databases and ACID transactions to guarantee that money transfers, balance updates, and ledger entries are never lost, duplicated, or left in an inconsistent state.
— Product catalogs, shopping carts, order histories, and stock levels at companies like Amazon and Flipkart are built on top of relational databases queried constantly with SQL.
— Tools like Tableau, Power BI, and Looker connect directly to SQL databases and data warehouses, letting analysts write SQL (or generate it visually) to build dashboards and reports.
— Nearly every web application framework — Django, Ruby on Rails, Laravel, Spring Boot — uses SQL under the hood (often via an ORM) to store user accounts, content, and application state.
— Snowflake, Amazon Redshift, and Google BigQuery let organizations run SQL queries across petabytes of data for large-scale analytics, all while keeping the same familiar SQL syntax.
— SQLite, a lightweight embedded SQL database, ships inside nearly every Android and iOS app to store local data like settings, cached content, and offline records.
— Before any model training happens, data scientists use SQL to extract, clean, and join raw data from production databases into usable datasets for tools like Pandas or Spark.
— Electronic health records, patient management systems, and large government databases depend on SQL's strong consistency guarantees to keep sensitive records accurate and auditable.

sections.title: Why Should You Learn SQL in 2026?

blocks.text: Every year people ask — "Is SQL still worth learning with so many new tools around?" The answer in 2026 is a resounding YES. Here's why SQL should be one of the very first skills on your learning roadmap:

items.text: — Whether you become a software engineer, data analyst, product manager, or marketer, at some point you will need to query a database directly — SQL is the one skill that shows up across nearly every tech-adjacent career.
— SQL is consistently the single most requested skill in data analyst and data engineer job postings, often ranked above even Python or Excel.
— Because virtually every company runs on relational databases somewhere in its stack, SQL skills remain in demand across startups, enterprises, banks, and government alike.
— You can write useful SELECT, WHERE, and JOIN queries within your first few hours of practice — the payoff-to-effort ratio for beginners is among the best of any technical skill.
— SQL is not a competitor to Python, Excel, or BI tools — it strengthens all of them. Nearly every data pipeline, dashboard, and backend API eventually talks to a SQL database.
— PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite are all free and open-source, and countless free interactive SQL tutorials and sandboxes let you practice without installing anything.

blocks.text: SQL evolves through periodic ANSI/ISO standards, while individual database vendors ship their own release versions implementing (and extending) those standards. Understanding both is useful — especially when reading documentation or older tutorials:

items.text: — A hugely influential standard that most modern databases still treat as a rough compatibility baseline, introducing standardized joins and much of the syntax beginners learn first.
— Added recursive queries, triggers, and early support for more complex, object-oriented style data.
— Introduced window functions and XML-related features, unlocking powerful analytical queries directly inside SQL.
— Added native JSON functions, formally acknowledging the growing overlap between relational and document-style data.
— The latest ratified standard, adding native property graph query capabilities and further JSON improvements. Most engines only support parts of it, adopted gradually over time.
— The current major releases of the leading open-source and commercial engines in 2026, each layering performance improvements and modern data-type support on top of the shared SQL standard.

blocks.text: These are the most commonly asked SQL interview questions for freshers and beginner-level positions. Master these before any SQL or data-related interview.

items.q: Q1. What is SQL and what are its key characteristics?
items.a: SQL (Structured Query Language) is a declarative, standardized language used to define, manipulate, and query data stored in relational databases. Its key characteristics are: a declarative syntax where you describe what data you want rather than how to fetch it, strong support for ACID transactions, standardized core syntax under ANSI/ISO, and support for joins, aggregations, and constraints that enforce data integrity.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between a database engine, the SQL standard, and client tools?
items.a: A database engine (like MySQL or PostgreSQL) is the actual server software that stores data and executes your queries. The SQL standard is the shared language specification, maintained by ANSI/ISO, that defines common syntax across engines. Client tools, such as psql or DBeaver, are how developers actually write and send SQL to the engine and view the results. In short: the engine executes it, the standard defines it, client tools let you use it.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL?
items.a: DDL (Data Definition Language) defines database structure using commands like CREATE, ALTER, and DROP. DML (Data Manipulation Language) works with actual data using SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. DCL (Data Control Language) manages permissions with GRANT and REVOKE. TCL (Transaction Control Language) manages transactions using COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT. Together these four categories cover essentially everything you can do in SQL.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between a PRIMARY KEY and a FOREIGN KEY?
items.a: A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row in a table and cannot contain NULL values or duplicates. A FOREIGN KEY is a column (or set of columns) in one table that references the PRIMARY KEY of another table, enforcing referential integrity so you cannot insert a value that doesn't correspond to an existing row in the related table. Foreign keys are what let SQL model real-world relationships, like an order belonging to a specific customer.

items.q: Q5. What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
items.a: An INNER JOIN returns only the rows that have matching values in both tables being joined — non-matching rows are excluded entirely. A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, along with matching data from the right table where it exists, filling in NULL values for the right table's columns when there is no match. LEFT JOIN is commonly used when you want to keep all records from a primary table even if related data is missing.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
items.a: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping or aggregation happens, and cannot reference aggregate functions like COUNT() or SUM() directly. HAVING filters groups after a GROUP BY has been applied, and is specifically designed to filter based on aggregate results, such as HAVING COUNT(*) > 5. A common trap: trying to use an aggregate function inside a WHERE clause causes a SQL error — it belongs in HAVING instead.

items.q: Q7. What is database normalization?
items.a: Normalization is the process of organizing tables and columns to minimize data redundancy and prevent update anomalies, typically by breaking large tables into smaller, related ones connected via foreign keys. It follows a series of 'normal forms' (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and beyond), each adding stricter rules — for example, 1NF requires atomic column values, while 3NF removes columns that depend on non-key attributes.

items.q: Q8. What is a NULL value in SQL, and how is it different from zero or an empty string?
items.a: NULL represents the absence of a known value — it is not the same as zero (a numeric value) or an empty string (a valid but blank piece of text). Because NULL means 'unknown,' comparisons like column = NULL always evaluate to unknown (not true), which is why SQL requires the special IS NULL and IS NOT NULL operators to check for it correctly.

items.q: Q9. What is the latest SQL standard in 2026?
items.a: The current ratified standard is SQL:2023, which formally added native property graph query features and further JSON functionality on top of earlier standards like SQL:2016. In practice, most developers work against a specific database engine's version — such as PostgreSQL 17 or MySQL 8.4 — which implements a subset of the full ANSI/ISO standard plus its own vendor-specific extensions.

items.q: Q10. What is a subquery, and how is it different from a JOIN?
items.a: A subquery is a SQL query nested inside another query, often used inside a WHERE or FROM clause to filter or compute an intermediate result — for example, selecting customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 1000). A JOIN combines columns from two or more tables directly into a single result set. Subqueries are often more readable for simple filtering, while JOINs are typically more efficient and standard when you need columns from multiple tables in your final output.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of SQL fundamentals with these practice questions. Try to answer each one before revealing the answer — active recall is the most effective way to learn.

items.q: 1. What does ACID stand for, and why does it matter for a SQL database?
items.a: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. Atomicity guarantees a transaction either fully completes or fully rolls back. Consistency ensures the database moves between valid states. Isolation prevents concurrent transactions from interfering with each other. Durability guarantees committed data survives a crash. Together, ACID properties are why SQL databases are trusted for critical systems like banking, where a half-completed money transfer would be unacceptable.

items.q: 2. What is the output difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column_name) when the column contains NULL values?
items.a: COUNT(*) counts every row in the result set, regardless of NULL values in any column. COUNT(column_name) counts only the rows where that specific column is NOT NULL, silently skipping rows with a NULL in that column. This is a common source of subtle bugs when analysts assume both counts will always match.

items.q: 3. What is the minimum you need to start practicing SQL on a new computer?
items.a: You need a database engine (SQLite requires no installation at all — it's just a single file) and a way to run queries against it, such as the sqlite3 command-line tool or a free GUI client like DBeaver. For a more production-like setup, installing PostgreSQL or MySQL locally, or using a free-tier cloud database, is a common next step for beginners.

items.q: 4. What happens if you run a DELETE statement without a WHERE clause?
items.a: It deletes every single row in the table, not just some of them — a WHERE clause is what limits DELETE (and UPDATE) to specific rows. This is one of SQL's most infamous beginner mistakes and a strong argument for always testing destructive statements first with a SELECT using the exact same WHERE condition before switching to DELETE or UPDATE.

items.q: 5. Explain the difference between a clustered index and a non-clustered index.
items.a: A clustered index determines the actual physical order in which table data is stored on disk — a table can have only one clustered index, often built on the primary key. A non-clustered index is a separate structure that stores pointers back to the actual rows, allowing multiple non-clustered indexes per table without reordering the underlying data. Clustered indexes are typically fastest for range queries on the indexed column; non-clustered indexes are ideal for speeding up lookups on other frequently filtered columns.

items.q: 6. Why can two functionally identical SQL queries have very different execution times?
items.a: Because the query optimizer chooses an execution plan based on indexes, table statistics, and estimated row counts — not just the literal query text. Factors like missing indexes, outdated statistics, inefficient join order, or unnecessary type conversions in a WHERE clause can force the optimizer into a much slower plan even when two queries return identical results. Reading the query's EXPLAIN plan is the standard way to diagnose these differences.

items.q: 7. What is a Common Table Expression (CTE), and when would you use RECURSIVE?
items.a: A CTE, defined with WITH name AS (...), creates a temporary named result set that can be referenced later in the same query, improving readability compared to deeply nested subqueries. A RECURSIVE CTE repeatedly references itself to work with hierarchical data — such as traversing an employee-to-manager reporting chain or a category tree — until no more rows are produced, something a standard non-recursive query cannot express directly.

items.q: 8. What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
items.a: UNION combines the result sets of two queries and automatically removes duplicate rows, which requires an internal sort or hash step and therefore costs more performance. UNION ALL combines the result sets without removing duplicates, making it faster whenever you already know there won't be overlapping rows, or when duplicates are acceptable in the final output.

sections.title: Conclusion — Is SQL Right for You?

blocks.text: SQL is not just a programming language — it is the universal interface to structured data. From the banking systems that move trillions of dollars every day to the dashboards your marketing team checks every morning, from mobile apps storing data locally to petabyte-scale cloud data warehouses — SQL remains the common thread connecting them all.

If you are a complete beginner, SQL is one of the fastest technical skills to become genuinely useful with — you can be writing real, useful queries within hours. If you are already working in software development, data analysis, or business intelligence, SQL is not optional — it is one of the most consistently requested skills across nearly every related job posting.

SQL is over 50 years old — and still growing. With modern engines adding native JSON, vector search, and massive cloud-scale analytics on top of the same declarative foundation, SQL in 2026 is more relevant and more in-demand than ever before. Start today. 🗄️

items.q: Is SQL easy to learn for beginners?
items.a: Yes — SQL is widely regarded as one of the fastest technical skills to become useful with. Its English-like syntax means most beginners can write real, working SELECT, WHERE, and JOIN queries within their first few hours of practice. Mastering advanced topics like query optimization and window functions takes longer, but the basics are genuinely approachable for complete beginners.

items.q: What is the difference between SQL and MySQL?
items.a: SQL is the language itself — a standardized way to define and query relational data. MySQL is one specific database engine (software) that implements SQL, alongside others like PostgreSQL, Oracle Database, and SQL Server. Learning 'SQL' means learning the language; MySQL is just one of several places you can use it, each with its own extensions and quirks.

items.q: How long does it take to learn SQL?
items.a: With consistent daily practice, you can learn core SQL — SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, and basic aggregation — in about 2–3 weeks. Becoming comfortable with subqueries, window functions, and database design typically takes 1–2 months. Mastering advanced topics like query optimization, indexing strategy, and complex transaction handling can take 6 months to a year of real project experience.

items.q: Is SQL free to use in 2026?
items.a: The SQL language itself is a free, open standard. Whether the software is free depends on the database engine you choose: PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite are completely free and open-source, while Oracle Database and Microsoft SQL Server offer paid enterprise editions alongside free or limited tiers for learning and small-scale use.

items.q: Should I learn PostgreSQL or MySQL in 2026?
items.a: Both are excellent, free, open-source choices with very similar core SQL syntax. PostgreSQL is often favoured for its advanced features, strict standards compliance, and growing popularity in modern data and analytics stacks. MySQL remains extremely widespread, especially in web development and existing legacy systems. Learning one makes picking up the other straightforward.

items.q: SQL vs NoSQL — Which is better in 2026?
items.a: Both remain essential and are often used together rather than as strict competitors. Choose SQL when your data is structured, relationships matter, and you need strong transactional guarantees, such as financial records or order management. Choose NoSQL (like MongoDB) when your data is highly variable, rapidly changing, or needs to scale horizontally across many servers with looser consistency requirements, such as activity feeds or session storage.
